# dplyr Helpers {#dplyr-helper-functions}

## Introduction

In this chapter, we will explore a set of helper functions in order to:

- extract unique rows 
- rename columns
- sample data
- extract columns
- slice rows
- arrange rows
- compare tables
- extract/mutate data using predicate functions
- count observations for different levels of a variable

We will use the following R packages:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
```
:::








## Case Study

Let us look at a case study (e-commerce data) and see how we can use dplyr 
helper functions to answer questions we have about and to modify/transform the 
underlying data set. 

### Data








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom <- 
  read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/web.csv',
    col_types = cols_only(device = col_factor(levels = c("laptop", "tablet", "mobile")),
      referrer = col_factor(levels = c("bing", "direct", "social", "yahoo", "google")),
      purchase = col_logical(), bouncers = col_logical(), duration = col_double(),
      n_visit = col_double(), n_pages = col_double()
    )
  )

ecom
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1,000 x 7
   referrer device bouncers n_visit n_pages duration purchase
   <fct>    <fct>  <lgl>      <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>   
 1 google   laptop TRUE          10       1      693 FALSE   
 2 yahoo    tablet TRUE           9       1      459 FALSE   
 3 direct   laptop TRUE           0       1      996 FALSE   
 4 bing     tablet FALSE          3      18      468 TRUE    
 5 yahoo    mobile TRUE           9       1      955 FALSE   
 6 yahoo    laptop FALSE          5       5      135 FALSE   
 7 yahoo    mobile TRUE          10       1       75 FALSE   
 8 direct   mobile TRUE          10       1      908 FALSE   
 9 bing     mobile FALSE          3      19      209 FALSE   
10 google   mobile TRUE           6       1      208 FALSE   
# i 990 more rows
```


:::
:::








### Data Dictionary

- referrer: referrer website/search engine
- device: device used to visit the website
- bouncers: whether a visit bounced (exited from landing page)
- duration: time spent on the website (in seconds)
- purchase: whether visitor purchased
- n_visit: number of visits
- n_pages: number of pages visited/browsed

## Data Sanitization

Let us ensure that the data is sanitized by checking the sources of traffic
and devices used to visit the site. We will use `distinct` to examine the
values in the `referrer` column








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/distinct_1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
distinct(ecom, referrer)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 x 1
  referrer
  <fct>   
1 google  
2 yahoo   
3 direct  
4 bing    
5 social  
```


:::
:::








and the `device` column as well.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
distinct(ecom, device)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 x 1
  device
  <fct> 
1 laptop
2 tablet
3 mobile
```


:::
:::








## Rename Columns

Columns can be renamed using `rename()`. 








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/rename_1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rename(ecom, time_on_site = duration)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1,000 x 7
   referrer device bouncers n_visit n_pages time_on_site purchase
   <fct>    <fct>  <lgl>      <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl> <lgl>   
 1 google   laptop TRUE          10       1          693 FALSE   
 2 yahoo    tablet TRUE           9       1          459 FALSE   
 3 direct   laptop TRUE           0       1          996 FALSE   
 4 bing     tablet FALSE          3      18          468 TRUE    
 5 yahoo    mobile TRUE           9       1          955 FALSE   
 6 yahoo    laptop FALSE          5       5          135 FALSE   
 7 yahoo    mobile TRUE          10       1           75 FALSE   
 8 direct   mobile TRUE          10       1          908 FALSE   
 9 bing     mobile FALSE          3      19          209 FALSE   
10 google   mobile TRUE           6       1          208 FALSE   
# i 990 more rows
```


:::
:::








## Data Tabulation

Let us now look at the proportion or share of visits driven by different sources
of traffic. 








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/tally_count.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom |>
  group_by(referrer) |>
  tally()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 x 2
  referrer     n
  <fct>    <int>
1 bing       194
2 direct     191
3 social     200
4 yahoo      207
5 google     208
```


:::
:::








We would also like to know the number of bouncers driven by the different 
sources of traffic.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom |>
  group_by(referrer, bouncers) |>
  tally()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 10 x 3
# Groups:   referrer [5]
   referrer bouncers     n
   <fct>    <lgl>    <int>
 1 bing     FALSE      104
 2 bing     TRUE        90
 3 direct   FALSE       98
 4 direct   TRUE        93
 5 social   FALSE       93
 6 social   TRUE       107
 7 yahoo    FALSE      110
 8 yahoo    TRUE        97
 9 google   FALSE      101
10 google   TRUE       107
```


:::
:::








Let us look at how many conversions happen across different devices.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom |>
  group_by(device, purchase) |>
  tally() |>
  filter(purchase)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 x 3
# Groups:   device [3]
  device purchase     n
  <fct>  <lgl>    <int>
1 laptop TRUE        31
2 tablet TRUE        36
3 mobile TRUE        36
```


:::
:::








Another way to extract the above information is by using `count`








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom |>
  count(referrer, purchase) |>
  filter(purchase)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 x 3
  referrer purchase     n
  <fct>    <lgl>    <int>
1 bing     TRUE        17
2 direct   TRUE        25
3 social   TRUE        20
4 yahoo    TRUE        22
5 google   TRUE        19
```


:::
:::








The `group_by()` + `tally()` pairs above can also be written with the `.by`
argument, which groups only for that verb and leaves the data ungrouped
afterwards:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = referrer)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 x 2
  referrer     n
  <fct>    <int>
1 google     208
2 yahoo      207
3 direct     191
4 bing       194
5 social     200
```


:::
:::








Two more helpers round out grouped work. `summarise()` must return a single
row per group; when a summary needs several rows, use `reframe()` instead:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom |>
  reframe(quartile = quantile(n_pages, c(0.25, 0.75)), .by = purchase)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 x 2
  purchase quartile
  <lgl>       <dbl>
1 FALSE           1
2 FALSE           8
3 TRUE           13
4 TRUE           18
```


:::
:::








And `pick()` bundles columns into a data frame inside a verb, so a computation
needing several columns at once does not repeat the data name:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom |>
  summarise(cor = with(pick(n_pages, duration), cor(n_pages, duration)), .by = purchase)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 x 2
  purchase    cor
  <lgl>     <dbl>
1 FALSE    -0.251
2 TRUE      0.429
```


:::
:::








## Sampling Data

dplyr offers a sampling function which allows us to specify either the
number or percentage of observations. `slice_sample()` allows sampling a specific
number of observations.  








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/sample_frac_n.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
slice_sample(ecom, n = 700)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 700 x 7
   referrer device bouncers n_visit n_pages duration purchase
   <fct>    <fct>  <lgl>      <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>   
 1 direct   mobile FALSE          1       9      135 FALSE   
 2 direct   mobile TRUE           5       1      352 FALSE   
 3 social   mobile TRUE          10       1      479 FALSE   
 4 direct   tablet FALSE          8      16      192 FALSE   
 5 social   tablet FALSE          5      10      200 FALSE   
 6 yahoo    laptop FALSE          5      11      143 FALSE   
 7 yahoo    tablet FALSE          8      14      322 FALSE   
 8 yahoo    mobile TRUE           8       1      160 FALSE   
 9 yahoo    mobile FALSE          3      20      480 FALSE   
10 bing     tablet FALSE          3      15      390 TRUE    
# i 690 more rows
```


:::
:::








We can combine the sampling function with grouping as shown below
where we sample observations after grouping them according to the source of
traffic.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
slice_sample(ecom, n = 100, by = referrer)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 500 x 7
   referrer device bouncers n_visit n_pages duration purchase
   <fct>    <fct>  <lgl>      <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>   
 1 google   laptop TRUE           3       1      193 FALSE   
 2 google   mobile FALSE          5       7      133 FALSE   
 3 google   tablet TRUE           8       1      891 FALSE   
 4 google   tablet TRUE           8       1      301 FALSE   
 5 google   laptop TRUE           3       1      369 FALSE   
 6 google   laptop TRUE           5       1      951 FALSE   
 7 google   mobile FALSE          1      20      320 FALSE   
 8 google   tablet TRUE           6       1      250 FALSE   
 9 google   laptop FALSE          0       3       45 FALSE   
10 google   laptop FALSE         10      18      450 FALSE   
# i 490 more rows
```


:::
:::








`slice_sample()` with the `prop` argument allows sampling a specific percentage of observations.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
slice_sample(ecom, prop = 0.7)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 700 x 7
   referrer device bouncers n_visit n_pages duration purchase
   <fct>    <fct>  <lgl>      <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>   
 1 yahoo    mobile FALSE          5       3       30 FALSE   
 2 social   mobile TRUE           5       1      527 FALSE   
 3 direct   laptop TRUE           2       1      384 FALSE   
 4 social   tablet TRUE           1       1      566 FALSE   
 5 bing     mobile FALSE          3      15      450 FALSE   
 6 google   laptop TRUE           1       1      958 FALSE   
 7 bing     laptop TRUE           4       1      750 FALSE   
 8 direct   tablet TRUE           4       1      164 FALSE   
 9 google   mobile FALSE          5      13      390 FALSE   
10 social   tablet TRUE           5       1      752 FALSE   
# i 690 more rows
```


:::
:::








## Data Extraction

In the first [chapter](https://blog.aravindhebbali.com/2017/12/25/data-wrangling-with-dplyr-part-1/),
we had observed that dplyr verbs always returned a tibble. What if you want to
extract a specific column or a bunch of rows but not as a tibble? 

Use `pull` to extract columns either by name or position. It will return a 
vector. In the below example, we extract the `device` column as a vector. I am 
using `head` in addition to limit the output printed.

### Sample Data








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom_mini <- slice_sample(ecom, n = 10)
```
:::

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/pull_1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pull(ecom_mini, device)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] tablet tablet laptop mobile mobile laptop tablet tablet mobile tablet
Levels: laptop tablet mobile
```


:::
:::








Let us extract the first column from `ecom` using column position instead of 
name.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pull(ecom_mini, 1) 
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] social yahoo  google direct bing   social bing   direct google yahoo 
Levels: bing direct social yahoo google
```


:::
:::








You can use `-` before the column position to indicate the position in reverse.
The below example extracts data from the last column.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pull(ecom_mini, -1) 
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE
```


:::
:::








Let us now look at extracting rows using `slice()`. In the below example, we 
extract data starting from the 5th row and upto the 15th row.








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/slice_1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
slice(ecom, 5:15)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 11 x 7
   referrer device bouncers n_visit n_pages duration purchase
   <fct>    <fct>  <lgl>      <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>   
 1 yahoo    mobile TRUE           9       1      955 FALSE   
 2 yahoo    laptop FALSE          5       5      135 FALSE   
 3 yahoo    mobile TRUE          10       1       75 FALSE   
 4 direct   mobile TRUE          10       1      908 FALSE   
 5 bing     mobile FALSE          3      19      209 FALSE   
 6 google   mobile TRUE           6       1      208 FALSE   
 7 direct   laptop TRUE           9       1      738 FALSE   
 8 direct   tablet FALSE          6      12      132 FALSE   
 9 direct   mobile FALSE          9      14      406 TRUE    
10 yahoo    tablet FALSE          5       8       80 FALSE   
11 yahoo    mobile FALSE          7       1       19 FALSE   
```


:::
:::








Use `n()` inside `slice()` to extract the last row.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
slice(ecom, n())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1 x 7
  referrer device bouncers n_visit n_pages duration purchase
  <fct>    <fct>  <lgl>      <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>   
1 google   mobile TRUE           9       1      269 FALSE   
```


:::
:::








## Between

`between()` allows us to test if the values in a column lie between two specific
values. In the below example, we check how many visits browsed pages between 5 
and 15.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom_sample <- slice_sample(ecom, n = 30)
  
ecom_sample |>
  pull(n_pages) |>
  between(5, 15) 
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE
[13]  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE
[25] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE
```


:::
:::








## Case When

`case_when()` is an alternative to `if else`. It allows us to lay down the 
conditions clearly and makes the code more readable. In the below example, we
create a new column `repeat_visit` from `n_visit` (the number of previous visits).








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom |>
  mutate(
    repeat_visit = case_when(
      n_visit > 0 ~ TRUE,
      TRUE ~ FALSE
    )
  ) |>
  select(n_visit, repeat_visit) 
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1,000 x 2
   n_visit repeat_visit
     <dbl> <lgl>       
 1      10 TRUE        
 2       9 TRUE        
 3       0 FALSE       
 4       3 TRUE        
 5       9 TRUE        
 6       5 TRUE        
 7      10 TRUE        
 8      10 TRUE        
 9       3 TRUE        
10       6 TRUE        
# i 990 more rows
```


:::
:::
